**Core difference: what history look like after.**

Merge — makes new commit with two parents. Both branch histories stay intact. Nothing rewritten.

```
main:    A---B---C---M
                    /
feature:   D---E---F
```

Rebase — replays your commits on top of new base. Old commits discarded, new ones created with new hashes. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
main:    A---B---C---D'---E'---F'
```

Key: rebase does **not** move commits. Copies them. `D'` different commit than `D` — different hash, different parent, same diff.

**Conflicts differ too.** Merge resolves once, at merge commit. Rebase replays commit-by-commit — same conflict can reappear at each commit. Painful for long branches.

## When rebase

- Update your local feature branch onto latest `main` before opening PR. `git rebase main`
- Clean up your own messy WIP commits before sharing. `git rebase -i HEAD~5`
- Team wants linear history, bisect-friendly.

## When merge

- Merging feature into shared branch (`main`, `develop`).
- Branch already pushed and others pulled it.
- Long-lived branch with many conflicts — merge once beats replay ten times.
- Want to preserve real record of when work happened.

## Hard rule

**Never rebase commits others already pulled.** Rewritten hashes force everyone else to fix their history — recovery is manual and error-prone. Rebase only commits that live solely on your machine or on a branch only you use.

Practical setup: rebase locally to stay current, merge to integrate.

```bash
git config --global pull.rebase true   # pull rebases instead of merging
git merge --no-ff feature              # integration keeps merge commit
```

`--no-ff` forces merge commit even when fast-forward possible — keeps branch boundary visible.
